post.caption: This amber can turn blue in sunlight. Most blue amber is mined in the Dominican Republic, in the north near the city of Santiago. Its age is debated, but 15 to 20 million years is common. The blue is fluorescence, set off by the ultraviolet light in sunlight, and it shows best against a dark background. Hold it up to the light and it looks plain yellow, because the blue sits on the surface of the stone. A hydrocarbon called perylene is the likely cause, and blue amber costs more than ordinary amber. Amber floats in salt water, which helps expose glass fakes.
